prime.problem: The same request never takes the same time twice, and dashboards usually show the median. An agent makes dozens of calls, so it almost certainly hits the slow end of the distribution that the median hides.
prime.fits: First agent card. The harness card turned one call into N calls; this card shows what N does to your odds of hitting a slow one. Retries and parallel calls, later, build on the same tail.
prime.goal: Read a latency distribution, compute how often a multi-call task hits the tail, and pick a defence.

attend: Why did 20 identical 60-token runs on one idle-ish laptop range from 3.19 s to 7.14 s?
Why can a provider with a good median be a bad pick for an agent?
Why does the chance of hitting the slowest 1% rise so fast with the number of calls?
What does a hedged request buy, and when is it unsafe?

must: Identical requests take varying time (load, heat, other users) → sort them into percentiles → the median hides a slow tail (p99 up to 20× p50 on hosted APIs)
An agent makes N calls on its critical path → the chance at least one is slow = 1 − (1 − q)<sup>N</sup> → 50 calls hit the slowest 1% 39.5% of the time → agents live in the tail
One slow call on the path delays the whole task (6.1 s → 17.9 s for 10 calls) → budget p95/p99, not the mean → hedge: send a backup after the p95 wait and take whichever returns first
elevated: Hedging adds at most ~5% extra calls when fired after the p95 wait → but does nothing for shared slowness (outage, huge prompt) and duplicates side effects → use timeout + fallback for those
reference: Dean & Barroso's 1,800 ms → 74 ms p99.9 result

compress.prompt: From memory, define p50, p95 and p99 in one line each, write the formula for the chance a task of N calls hits the slowest 1%, and compute it for N = 10 and 100. Then list two defences and when each fails.
checklist: percentiles: sort the times; p50 middle, p95 and p99 near the top
one slow call on the critical path stretches the whole task
measure and budget p95/p99; hedge after the p95 wait
hedging fails on shared slowness and is unsafe with side effects

retrieve.q: Explain why optimising the average latency can leave an agent slow in practice.
answer: the average hides rare slow calls
an agent makes many calls, so it hits a rare slow call often
task time follows the slowest call on its critical path, not the average

retrieve.q: Walk through the 20-run M3 measurement: how p50 and p95 are computed from the sorted list, and why 20 runs can't give a p99.
answer: p99 needs the slowest 1%: with 20 samples there aren't enough points

retrieve.q: Choose between Baseten (p50 0.33 s, p99 3.23 s) and Together AI (p50 0.61 s, p99 12.45 s) for a 50-call agent, and for an overnight batch job.
answer: agent: Baseten; with 50 calls the p99 is likely hit, and Baseten's tail is ~4× shorter
batch: the median and cost matter more; the tail averages out
either way, check failure rates, which the percentiles exclude

compare.q: Running calls in parallel cuts the wait from the sum to the maximum. Why does that same "wait for the slowest" make the tail more dangerous?
answer: the task waits for the slowest of N parallel calls
the chance at least one is slow rises with N
so fan-out trades a shorter typical wait for more exposure to the tail

compare.q: Server SLOs are usually set on p99 TTFT or TPOT. Why do servers and agent builders both reach for the tail rather than the mean, and what does each do about it?
answer: both serve many requests, so rare slow ones are common in absolute terms
servers: scheduling, admission and preemption to cap the tail
agents: hedging, timeouts, fallbacks and fewer calls on the critical path

predict.q: An agent's calls are each slow (past p95) 5% of the time, independently. Predict the chance a 30-call task hits at least one slow call before computing. Is it closer to 15%, 50% or 80%?
predict.answer: 1 − 0.95<sup>30</sup> ≈ 1 − 0.215 = 78.5%, so close to 80%. Adding the chances (30 × 5%) would give an impossible 150%; the product rule gives 78.5%. At 30 calls, hitting a p95-slow call is the normal case, not the exception.

apply.task: Measure your own tail. Send the same short request 30 times (local or hosted), record end-to-end times, sort them, and compute p50, p95 and max. Then compute the chance a 20-call task hits a call slower than your p95, and the task time if one call lands at your max.
apply.done: You have sorted times with p50, p95 and max, the probability 1 − 0.95<sup>20</sup> ≈ 64%, and a task-time estimate using 19 × p50 + 1 × max.
apply.hint: With 30 samples, p95 is roughly the 29th value; don't try to estimate p99.
